questions.stem: Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed by God to the Prophet Muhammad, beginning around 610 CE, near which city?
options: Mecca
Medina
Jerusalem
Baghdad
questions.explanation: Muhammad was born in Mecca, a trading city in western Arabia, and Muslims believe he received his first revelation in a cave on a mountain nearby around 610. Medina was the city he later moved to in 622. Baghdad was not founded until 762.

questions.stem: What was the Hijra?
options: The capture of Jerusalem by Muslim armies in the 630s
The split in the Muslim community between Sunni and Shia
The migration of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina in 622
The pilgrimage to Mecca that every Muslim who is able should make once in their life
questions.explanation: Facing persecution in Mecca, Muhammad and his followers moved to Medina in 622, where he led a growing community; the Islamic calendar counts its years from this event. The pilgrimage to Mecca is the Hajj, one of the Five Pillars. Muhammad returned to Mecca in 630, and the city surrendered with little fighting.

questions.stem: Which list gives the Five Pillars of Islam?
options: Prayer, charity, fasting in Ramadan, pilgrimage to Mecca and building a mosque
Declaration of faith, prayer, charity, pilgrimage to Mecca and visiting Jerusalem
Declaration of faith, prayer, charity, fasting in Ramadan and pilgrimage to Mecca
Declaration of faith, prayer, fasting in Ramadan, pilgrimage to Mecca and learning Arabic
questions.explanation: The Five Pillars are the shahada (declaration of faith), salat (prayer five times a day), zakat (giving to those in need), sawm (fasting in Ramadan) and the Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca for those able). Learning Arabic, building mosques and visiting Jerusalem can be important to Muslims, but they are not among the Five Pillars. Charity is the pillar most often left out by mistake.

questions.stem: In Islamic history, what was a caliph?
options: A successor to Muhammad as leader of the Muslim community, but not a prophet
A new prophet believed to be chosen by God to receive further revelations after Muhammad
A judge who decided cases in a local court using Islamic law
A tax collector who gathered the jizya from Christians and Jews
questions.explanation: Caliph comes from the Arabic khalifa, 'successor': caliphs led the Muslim community in religious and political matters after Muhammad's death in 632. Muslims regard Muhammad as the final prophet, so caliphs did not receive new revelations. The area and government ruled by a caliph is called a caliphate.

questions.stem: Who became the first caliph after Muhammad's death in 632?
options: Ali
Mu'awiya
Harun al-Rashid
Abu Bakr
questions.explanation: Abu Bakr, Muhammad's close companion and father-in-law, was chosen as the first of the four 'Rightly Guided' (Rashidun) caliphs, followed by Umar, Uthman and Ali. Shia Muslims believe Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, should have led from the start. Mu'awiya founded the Umayyad dynasty and Harun al-Rashid was a later Abbasid caliph.

questions.stem: How did the division between Sunni and Shia Muslims begin?
options: As a disagreement over who should lead the Muslim community after Muhammad's death
As a disagreement over whether Muslims should pray facing Jerusalem or Mecca
As a dispute between Arabs and Persians over which language the Qur'an should use
As a quarrel over whether the fast of Ramadan should last for one month or for two
questions.explanation: Shia Muslims (from Shi'at Ali, 'the party of Ali') held that leadership belonged to Ali and his descendants, while the majority, who became known as Sunni, accepted the caliphs chosen by the community. The split deepened after Ali's son Husayn was killed at Karbala in 680. Both groups pray towards Mecca and share the Five Pillars.

questions.stem: The Umayyad caliphs (661–750) ruled their empire from which city?
options: Córdoba
Cairo
Damascus
Baghdad
questions.explanation: The Umayyads moved the capital to Damascus in Syria. Baghdad was built later as the capital of the Abbasids, who overthrew the Umayyads in 750. A surviving Umayyad prince fled to Spain and founded a separate Umayyad state at Córdoba in 756, after the dates in the question.

questions.stem: The Dome of the Rock, completed under the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik around 691, stands in which city?
options: Jerusalem
Mecca
Damascus
Medina
questions.explanation: The Dome of the Rock was built in Jerusalem on the Temple Mount (Haram al-Sharif), a place sacred to Jews, Christians and Muslims, and is one of the oldest surviving Islamic buildings. Its gold dome and mosaics of plants and Arabic writing, with no images of people, influenced later Islamic art. Damascus has its own great Umayyad Mosque.

questions.stem: In 711, Umayyad forces crossed from North Africa and within a few years conquered most of:
options: the Italian peninsula, including the city of Rome
Greece and the city of Constantinople
Britain and the north of France
the Iberian Peninsula (Spain and Portugal)
questions.explanation: Led by Tariq ibn Ziyad, Umayyad armies crossed the strait now named after him (Gibraltar, from Jabal Tariq) and conquered most of Iberia, which Muslims called al-Andalus. Muslim rule continued in parts of Spain until 1492. Constantinople resisted Umayyad sieges and remained Byzantine until 1453.

questions.stem: European writers once claimed that the Battle of Tours (732), where the Frankish leader Charles Martel defeated an Umayyad army, saved Christian Europe. How do many historians now see it?
options: As a real defeat that ended raids into Francia, but less decisive than later writers claimed
As a great Umayyad victory that placed the kingdom of the Franks under Muslim rule
As a battle invented by later writers, since no sources from the time ever mention it at all
As the event that brought about the immediate collapse of the Umayyad caliphate
questions.explanation: Charles Martel's victory did stop a major raid, but many historians argue the Umayyads were already overstretched and that the battle's importance was exaggerated later, especially by writers who saw it as a clash of civilisations. The Umayyad caliphate fell in 750 because of the Abbasid revolution in the east, not because of Tours. The battle is mentioned in sources from the 700s.

questions.stem: Which city did the Abbasid caliphs build as their new capital in 762?
options: Istanbul
Baghdad
Damascus
Cairo
questions.explanation: The caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad on the Tigris River, designed as a round city, and it quickly grew into one of the largest and richest cities in the world. Damascus had been the Umayyad capital. Cairo was founded in 969 by the rival Fatimid dynasty.

questions.stem: What was the House of Wisdom in Abbasid Baghdad?
options: The great mosque where the caliph himself led the Friday prayers
A military school that trained officers for the caliph
A library and centre of learning where scholars translated and studied books
The caliph's palace, where foreign ambassadors were received with great ceremony
questions.explanation: Supported by caliphs such as al-Ma'mun, scholars in Baghdad translated Greek, Persian and Indian works on mathematics, medicine, astronomy and philosophy into Arabic and built on them with their own discoveries. Historians still debate how large and formal the institution was, but Baghdad was clearly a great centre of learning. Many of these works later reached Europe in Latin translations.

questions.stem: The word 'algebra' comes from the title of a book by which scholar of Baghdad?
options: Ibn Sina
Ibn Battuta
Saladin
al-Khwarizmi
questions.explanation: Al-Khwarizmi's book on calculation by 'al-jabr' (restoring and balancing equations), written in the 800s, gave algebra its name, and the word 'algorithm' comes from his own name. Ibn Sina was a physician and philosopher. Ibn Battuta was a traveller of the 1300s, and Saladin was a sultan and military leader.

questions.stem: Why are the numerals 0 to 9 that we use today called Hindu–Arabic numerals?
options: They were developed in India and passed to Europe through Arabic-speaking scholars
They were invented in Arabia and later copied by Indian merchants trading spices
They were brought from India to Europe by Roman traders during the time of the empire
They were invented in medieval Italy and given Arabic names to make them more popular
questions.explanation: Indian mathematicians developed place-value numerals with a zero; scholars such as al-Khwarizmi adopted and explained them, and they spread in Europe through Latin translations of Arabic works from the 1100s. Before that, Europeans mostly used Roman numerals, which made calculation slow. The Romans had no knowledge of this system.

questions.stem: Ibn Sina (known in Europe as Avicenna) is best known for:
options: Leading the Muslim army that recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders
The Canon of Medicine, a textbook used in European universities for centuries
Drawing the first map of the world to show the Americas and Australia
Founding the round city of Baghdad on the banks of the Tigris River in the year 762
questions.explanation: Ibn Sina, a Persian physician and philosopher who died in 1037, wrote the Canon of Medicine, which gathered Greek, Persian and Arabic medical knowledge with his own observations; translated into Latin, it was taught in European universities into the 1600s. Baghdad was founded by al-Mansur, and Jerusalem was recaptured by Saladin.

questions.stem: Paper-making spread into the Islamic world from China in the 700s. Why did this matter?
options: It allowed Baghdad to build the world's first printing presses with movable metal type
It ended the use of the astrolabe, because star charts could now be printed
Cheaper writing material helped books, libraries and government records multiply
It meant that the Arabic alphabet could be replaced with Chinese characters
questions.explanation: Paper was much cheaper than parchment or papyrus, so after paper mills were set up in places such as Baghdad, books, libraries, bookshops and official records spread rapidly. Arabic script continued to be used. Gutenberg's printing press, with movable metal type, came much later, in Europe in the 1400s.

questions.stem: Muslim scholars improved the astrolabe. What was it used for?
options: Finding the positions of stars to tell the time, find latitude and locate Mecca
Looking closely at distant planets and moons through a pair of magnifying glass lenses
Finding north at sea using a needle that had been rubbed with a magnet
Measuring the passing hours by the steady flow of water from a bowl
questions.explanation: The astrolabe, first developed by the ancient Greeks, was refined by Muslim astronomers to measure the height of the sun and stars, which allowed them to tell the time, work out latitude and find the direction of Mecca (the qibla) for prayer. Telescopes were invented in Europe in the 1600s, and the magnetic compass came from China. Astrolabes later reached Europe through al-Andalus.

questions.stem: Under the caliphates, Jews and Christians were usually treated as dhimmi. What did this mean?
options: They were banned from trade, government jobs and scholarship
They were protected and could keep their faith, but paid the jizya tax
They were forced to convert to Islam or else leave Muslim lands
They had exactly the same rights and paid the same taxes as Muslim subjects
questions.explanation: Dhimmi ('protected people') could practise their religion and run many of their own community affairs, in return for paying the jizya and accepting certain restrictions. They were not equal to Muslims, but forced conversion was not the usual policy. Many Jews and Christians worked as officials, doctors and translators, including in the House of Wisdom.

questions.stem: How did Islam spread to places such as the East African coast and West Africa?
options: Through Mongol armies that converted the lands they conquered in Africa
Largely through Muslim merchants trading across the Indian Ocean and the Sahara
Only through conquest by the armies sent out by the caliph in Baghdad
Through Christian missionaries sent out by the Byzantine emperors in Constantinople
questions.explanation: Muslim traders sailed the monsoon winds across the Indian Ocean and crossed the Sahara in camel caravans, trading gold, salt, textiles and other goods; local rulers and merchants often adopted Islam through these contacts. The caliphs' armies never conquered these regions. Cities such as Kilwa and Timbuktu became centres of Islamic trade and learning.

questions.stem: Córdoba, in al-Andalus, is often described as one of the greatest cities of Europe in the 900s. What supports this description?
options: It was the capital of the Abbasid caliphs and home of the House of Wisdom
It was ruled by the Byzantine emperor and was the largest Christian city
It was founded by the Ottomans after they conquered the Iberian Peninsula
Its Great Mosque, large libraries and many scholars and poets
questions.explanation: Under the Umayyad rulers of al-Andalus, who declared their own caliphate in 929, Córdoba had a huge population, the Great Mosque and large libraries, and scholars of different faiths worked there. The Abbasid capital was Baghdad. The Ottomans never ruled Spain.

questions.stem: Why were the Crusaders able to capture Jerusalem in 1099, according to many historians?
options: Jerusalem had no walls or soldiers, so the Crusaders simply walked in
The Mongols had already destroyed the Muslim armies of the region
Muslim rulers in Syria and Egypt were divided and fighting among themselves
The Abbasid caliph handed the city over in a treaty to avoid a long and costly war
questions.explanation: The rival Seljuk Turks and the Fatimid dynasty of Egypt were competing for control of Syria and Palestine, and local rulers were too divided to unite against the Crusaders. Jerusalem was walled and defended, and fell after a siege followed by a massacre of many of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants. The Mongols arrived in the region only in the 1200s.

questions.stem: Saladin is remembered in both Muslim and European sources. What did he do in 1187?
options: He led the First Crusade and then set up the Christian Kingdom of Jerusalem there
He sacked Baghdad and brought the Abbasid caliphate to an end
He recaptured Jerusalem and let many Christians ransom themselves and leave
He captured Constantinople and brought the Byzantine Empire to an end
questions.explanation: After defeating the Crusader army at Hattin in 1187, Saladin retook Jerusalem; instead of a massacre like that of 1099, many inhabitants were allowed to ransom themselves and leave. This earned him respect even among his enemies, and he later fought Richard I of England in the Third Crusade. Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453, and Baghdad to the Mongols in 1258.

questions.stem: Which event in 1258 ended the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad?
options: The Ottoman Turks captured the city after a long siege
Mongol forces under Hülegü captured and sacked the city
Crusader armies captured the city and killed the last caliph
Saladin overthrew the last caliph and ruled from Cairo
questions.explanation: Hülegü, a grandson of Genghis Khan, besieged and sacked Baghdad in 1258, killing the caliph and a huge number of its people and destroying libraries, including, according to later accounts, the books of the House of Wisdom. Crusaders never reached Baghdad, and Saladin died in 1193. The Ottomans did not take Baghdad until 1534.
